citation: Christoph RA, Buchanan L, Begalla K, Schwartz S. Pain reduction in local anesthetic administration through pH buffering. Ann Emerg Med 1988;17:117-120
text_quality: ok - all four pages present with a text layer (abstract, introduction, methods, results, Table 1, Table 2, the Figure legend, discussion, conclusion, acknowledgement and all 12 references). Two limits: the Figure is a bar chart of mean pain scores whose values exist only as plotted bars, so the per-solution pain means had to be read from the abstract and the discussion rather than from the Figure; and the OCR renders the half-minute symbols as 'V2'/'V~' (so 4 1/2 minutes appears as '4V2 minutes') and spaces out some words letter by letter. Nothing numeric is lost: Table 2 carries every area value and Table 1 every solution pH.
design: Randomised, prospective, double-blind, within-subject (paired) volunteer study. Every subject received all six solutions - three local anaesthetics each as a buffered and an unbuffered pair - one per site, at six sites. Pairs were assigned and labelled A to F from a random number table; the injector was blinded to which solution was which; a second investigator made the skin measurements. Analysis was Student's paired t test, buffered against unbuffered within each drug. There was no comparison between the three drugs and no placebo or saline arm.
population: 25 healthy adult volunteers aged 18 to 40. Pregnant subjects and anyone with a history of allergic or other adverse reaction to the study drugs, or a history of peripheral neuropathy, cardiovascular disease or hypertension, was excluded. Protocol approved by the University of Virginia Human Investigation Committee; informed consent obtained.
n: 25 subjects, all of whom completed. Within-subject design, so n = 25 for every one of the six solutions; 25 paired comparisons per drug.
setting: University of Virginia Medical Center, Emergency Medical Services, Charlottesville, Virginia. Healthy-volunteer laboratory study, not a patient series. Presented at the University Association for Emergency Medicine Annual Meeting, Philadelphia, May 1987.
intervention: Three local anaesthetics, each tested both buffered and unbuffered, so six solutions in all: 1% lidocaine, 1% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine, and 1% mepivacaine. The open question for this paper asks what this study itself used, so stated as what the study did: the mepivacaine arm was 0.5 mL of 1% mepivacaine per injection, delivered from a tuberculin syringe through a 25-gauge needle. Adulterant-free solutions intended for epidural block were used so as to avoid preservatives and additives. The study measured the pH of each resulting solution (Table 1): the three unbuffered solutions sat at 6.21, 5.98 and 6.18 and the three buffered ones at 7.22, 7.16 and 7.20. How the buffered solutions were made is a preparation matter and is not recorded here.
comparator: The unbuffered solution of the same drug, in the same subject, at a different site - a within-subject buffered-versus-unbuffered pair for each of the three drugs. No saline or placebo site and no head-to-head statistical comparison between the three drugs.
route: Intradermal. Each injection raised an intradermal wheal and was given over 2.5 seconds, timed by a metronome, by a blinded investigator through a 25-gauge needle. Volume per injection was the same at every site: 0.5 mL (recorded here because the paper's own open question asks what this study used). The six sites were the dorsum of the right hand, the dorsum of the left hand, the distal right volar forearm, the distal left volar forearm, the proximal right volar forearm and the proximal left volar forearm.
duration: This is the decisive point for the question asked of this paper. No duration of skin anaesthesia was measured. Skin measurement began 30 seconds after the injection and was repeated at 1, 1 1/2, 2 1/2, 3 1/2 and 4 1/2 minutes, and then stopped: the paper states that measures of skin anaesthesia were carried out for 4 1/2 minutes. What was recorded at each of those six readings was the area of skin anaesthetised to pinprick, not an onset time or an offset time. In Table 2 that area was still rising at the last reading for all six solutions, including both mepivacaine solutions (unbuffered mepivacaine 3.3, 4.4, 4.6, 5.8, 7.2 and 8.0 cm2 across the six readings; buffered mepivacaine 3.3, 4.1, 5.1, 6.3, 7.3 and 7.9 cm2), so no solution had been followed even to its peak extent, let alone to recovery. The abstract's sentence that onset, extent and duration of skin anaesthesia were not statistically altered by pH buffering is therefore not backed by any duration measurement in this paper: the duration half of it rests on the cited nerve-preparation, major-nerve-block and regional-nerve-block literature and on an uncontrolled clinical impression from the authors' own emergency department.
outcomes: Primary: pain of infiltration, each subject marking a linear 0-to-10 Visual Analogue Scale immediately after each injection (citing Scott and Huskisson 1976 for the instrument). Secondary (the paper's measure of anaesthetic efficacy): the area of skin anaesthetised to pinprick, obtained by marking the diameter of the pinprick-insensitive area on a 3-inch strip of cloth tape laid across the wheal at right angles to the needle axis, at six times in the first 4 1/2 minutes, then converting diameter to area in cm2 on the assumption that the wheal was a circle spreading as enlarging concentric circles. Also measured: the pH of each of the six solutions. Not measured: offset, recovery or total duration of anaesthesia; depth; blood flow; any outcome beyond 4 1/2 minutes.

funding_conflicts: No funding source and no conflict-of-interest statement appears anywhere in the paper. The only acknowledgement thanks two named physicians for editorial assistance with the manuscript.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Buckley FP, Duval Neto G, Fink BR. Acid and alkaline solutions of local anesthetics: duration of nerve block and tissue pH. Anesth Analg 1985;64:477-482
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: One of the three references Christoph cites for the claim that buffering leaves duration unchanged, described in the text as regional nerve block. Its abstract shows it is a rat infraorbital nerve-block study, so this leg of the support is animal and not human, and not in skin. Bears on D025 and on any page that reads Christoph 1988 as a duration measurement.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: DiFazio CA, Carron H, Grosslight KR, Moscicki JC, Bolding WR, Johns RA. Comparison of pH-adjusted lidocaine solutions for epidural anesthesia. Anesth Analg 1986;65:760-764
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: The second reference behind the same duration claim, described in the text as major nerve block. It is in fact an epidural study of 148 adult patients whose reported endpoints are onset of analgesia and of surgical anaesthesia, not duration and not skin. Bears on D025.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Galindo A. pH-adjusted local anesthetics: clinical experience. Reg Anesth 1983;8:35-36
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: The third reference behind the duration claim, a two-page clinical-experience note. Not indexed in Europe PMC (searched 2026-10-08, engine europepmc, hitCount 0), so its design cannot be checked from an abstract. Bears on D025 as the weakest leg of the paper's duration support.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Strobel GE, Bianchi CP. The effects of pH gradients on the distribution of C14-procaine and lidocaine in intact and desheathed sciatic nerve trunks. J Pharmacol Exp Ther 1970;172:18-32
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Cited as the nerve-preparation leg of the duration claim. It is an isolated-nerve drug-distribution experiment, not a duration study.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Scott J, Huskisson EC. Graphic representation of pain. Pain 1976;2:175-184
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: The source for the 0-to-10 linear Visual Analogue Scale used as this study's pain instrument; establishes that the pain endpoint is a validated VAS rather than an ad hoc scale.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Moore DC. The pH of local anesthetic solutions. Anesth Analg 1981;60:833-834
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Cited for the statement that marketed local anaesthetic solutions are acidic; the source of the pH range this study's Table 1 is measured against.
